name: Sara Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can give me the public answer and the private one. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Well, this time of year it's turkeys, morning to night. We rear two thousand bronze turkeys for Christmas, free-range in the orchard, and from now until the twenty-third it's feeding, checking, taking orders and planning the plucking. The rest of the year it's oats and wheat on two hundred acres and forty store cattle, which we buy young and sell on fattened. Patrick, my husband, hurt his back eight years ago, so he does the books and the phone, and our apprentice Megan, she's nineteen, does a bit of everything with me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like Christmas week, even though it nearly kills us. Families come to collect their bird, and the same faces come every year, some for twenty years. What wears me out is the long nights in December and the price of feed. I'll use one of those AI chat tools now and then to sort the order list, since my nephew showed me, but I'm not glued to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. I'd say it at the parish harvest supper, which I organise, so I'd get the last word. Most people at the supper would agree, they've seen fads come and go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be content. Turkeys don't read the news. They want feeding at seven whether the computers are clever or not. We've got money put by, the farm's ours, and the Christmas trade is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. We'd finish the new plucking shed we've been saving for, about twenty thousand. And I'd sign Megan up for her second year at the agricultural college on day release, which we pay half of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the plucking shed matter so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we've been plucking in the old cow shed with the wind coming through the slats for twenty-five years. Patrick says it's the one job he's glad his back got him out of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me a bit more about Megan.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She came from the college two years ago, couldn't tell a heifer from a steer, and now she's better with the turkeys than I am. I believe in apprentices. Somebody gave me a chance once, and you pass it on.

S0.say: It's what I expected, and most people at the harvest supper would agree. They've seen fads come and go.
S0.think: I'd be content. Turkeys want feeding at seven whether the computers are clever or not, and we've money put by, the farm's ours and the Christmas trade is steady.
S0.do: Carries on and finishes the long-planned plucking shed for about twenty thousand. Pays half of Megan's second year at agricultural college on day release.
S0.quote: Turkeys don't read the news. They want feeding at seven whether the computers are clever or not.
S0.fieldNote: Sara's farm runs on a seasonal rhythm built around Christmas turkeys and loyal families who collect every year. Her belief in apprenticeships is personal: 'somebody gave me a chance once'. In this picture she spends on the farm and on Megan's training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every new thing needs good people to run it, and that's what apprenticeships are for. I'd say businesses should train their own people rather than wait for the government. I'd say it at the supper and at the turkey collection, to whoever'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine. People don't want a robot-reared Christmas turkey, they want to shake the hand of the woman who raised it. The machines can have the oats. They can't have Christmas week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what the neighbours did with the arable side, and if a robot sprayer or weeder proved itself, I'd hire a contractor who had one. I'd use the chat tool more for the order list and maybe the cattle records. And I'd make sure Megan's college course covered the new machines, so she's ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little nudge of worry for Megan, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses should train their own people. What if a small farm can't afford to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they should club together. My father used to share a threshing gang with three farms. Three of us could share an apprentice and a machine. It doesn't have to be the government doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our Kieran works in a bank in the city, checking loans. That's the sort of job I hear goes first. I'd pray for him, and I'd tell him to come home for Christmas week and learn to pluck, just in case. He'd laugh.

S1.say: Every new thing needs good people to run it, and that's what apprenticeships are for. Businesses should train their own people rather than wait for the government.
S1.think: I'd be fine, because people want to shake the hand of the woman who raised their Christmas turkey. The machines can have the oats, but not Christmas week.
S1.do: Waits to see how neighbours fare with arable robots, then hires a contractor who has a proven one. Uses the AI chat tool more for orders and records and makes sure Megan's course covers new machines.
S1.feel: Calm, with a small nudge of worry for Megan.
S1.quote: The machines can have the oats. They can't have Christmas week.
S1.fieldNote: Sara divides her farm into the part machines can have (the arable) and the part they can't (the Christmas trade). Her answer to change is apprenticeships and neighbours clubbing together, not the state. Her worry goes to her son in a bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a much quicker one. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our own, families and parishes, because the government won't move fast enough. I'd say companies that bring in robots should keep training young people, not just sack them. I'd say it plainly, without shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd worry. If everyone's out of work by Christmas 2028, who's buying a free-range turkey at three times the supermarket price? My customers are teachers and builders and bank clerks. If they lose their wages, my Christmas goes with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the turkey numbers from two thousand to twelve hundred in the first year, so I'm not left with birds nobody can afford. I'd keep Megan on whatever happens and put a bit more aside in savings. And I'd tell Kieran and Bridget that if they need to come home, there's room, and there's work, even if it's plucking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be counting orders in the night, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Megan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her she's got a place here as long as I've got a farm, and that she should learn every machine the college has. She's nineteen. She'll see the end of all this, and I'd want her on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government won't move fast enough. Would you want them to try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to help families stay together and keep small businesses open, yes. Not to pay everyone to stay home. People need to work, it's good for the soul, robots or not.

S2.say: We need to look after our own, families and parishes, because the government won't move fast enough. Companies bringing in robots should keep training young people, not just sack them.
S2.think: I'd worry, because my customers are teachers, builders and bank clerks. If they lose their wages, my Christmas trade goes with them.
S2.do: Cuts turkey numbers from two thousand to twelve hundred in the first year. Keeps Megan on, saves more and tells her grown children there's room and work at home if they need it.
S2.feel: Anxious, counting orders in the night for the first time.
S2.quote: My customers are teachers and builders and bank clerks. If they lose their wages, my Christmas goes with them.
S2.fieldNote: Sara's risk isn't robots on her farm but her customers' wages, which pay for premium turkeys. She'd shrink the flock early. Her faith in work as 'good for the soul' shapes what help she'd accept from government: support for families and small businesses, not pay to stay home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for people to retrain if they put their minds to it. I'd say the parish should set up something to help people find new trades. I'd say farmers should take on more apprentices now, while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three, and the turkey trade would be Megan's to carry on, if she wanted. Five years is just long enough to turn a nineteen-year-old into a farmer who can run the robots and still pluck a turkey by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on a second apprentice next autumn. I'd buy a share in a robot sprayer with two neighbours once one's proved itself, maybe ten thousand each. And Patrick and I would start the paperwork to bring Megan in as a partner on the turkeys over a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a hopeful sort of way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bringing an apprentice in as a partner is unusual. Why Megan rather than your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Liam farms with his wife's family already, Bridget's a nurse and loves it, and Kieran would sooner eat a turkey than rear one. Megan wants it. Family's who turns up, in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the five-year version change your worry about customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. People would have time to find other work, and some would. Some wouldn't. I'd keep the flock at fifteen hundred and see how the orders went each year.

S3.say: Five years is long enough for people to retrain if they put their minds to it. The parish should help people find new trades, and farmers should take on more apprentices now.
S3.think: I'd be sixty-three and the turkey trade could be Megan's. Five years is long enough to turn her into a farmer who can run the robots and still pluck by hand.
S3.do: Takes on a second apprentice next autumn and buys a share in a proven robot sprayer with two neighbours for about ten thousand each. Starts bringing Megan in as a partner on the turkeys.
S3.quote: Five years is just long enough to turn a nineteen-year-old into a farmer who can run the robots and still pluck a turkey by hand.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Sara build a succession around her apprentice Megan rather than her children. 'Family's who turns up, in the end' is a striking line from a traditionalist. Her answer to automation is shared machines and more apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and there's no excuse for not getting ready. I'd say it at the supper, and the priest would probably say it better from the pulpit. Train the young ones, look after the old ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it's nearly nothing. I'll be sixty-eight, Megan will be running the turkeys, and I'll be doing the orders with Patrick. My only worry is whether people will still be spending at Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and hand over gradually to Megan, like in the five-year one but slower. I'd bring in machines on the arable side once they're cheap and proven. And I'd tell Kieran to spend the next few years learning a trade alongside his bank job, maybe at evening classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is two apprentices' worth of time. That's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Kieran take that advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd roll his eyes and say, Mum, it's all apps now. Then he'd come home at Christmas and pluck forty birds without complaining, because he always does. He's a good lad underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope Christmas week looks like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same faces in the yard, a bit older, with grandchildren. Megan doing the handing over, me doing the gossiping. A robot in the shed if it has to be, but the people in the yard.

S4.say: Ten years is a fair warning, so there's no excuse for not getting ready. Train the young ones and look after the old ones.
S4.think: For me it's nearly nothing: I'll be sixty-eight, with Megan running the turkeys. My only worry is whether people will still be spending at Christmas.
S4.do: Carries on and hands over gradually to Megan. Brings in arable machines once cheap and proven and urges her son Kieran to learn a trade at evening classes alongside his bank job.
S4.feel: Calm; ten years feels like enough.
S4.quote: Ten years is two apprentices' worth of time. That's enough.
S4.fieldNote: Sara measures time in apprentices: ten years is 'two apprentices' worth'. Her picture of 2036 is the same families collecting their turkeys, with a robot in the shed if it must be. Her lingering concern across the AGI scenarios is customers' spending power.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years means my customers lose their wages before anyone's ready, and the Christmas trade goes with them. What would help is the government backing small family businesses and apprenticeships, so young people can still learn a trade, and parishes and neighbours sticking together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why people come back every year. It isn't the turkey, honestly. It's that I remember their children's names, and a machine never will, however clever it gets.

headlineQuote: It isn't the turkey, honestly. It's that I remember their children's names, and a machine never will, however clever it gets.
portrait: Sara Walsh, 58, rears two thousand free-range bronze turkeys for Christmas alongside oats, wheat and store cattle, with her husband Patrick on the books and her apprentice Megan at her side. She's a traditional, churchgoing believer in apprenticeships and in families and parishes looking after their own. She uses an AI chat tool now and then for orders. Her own farm is secure; her worry is customers losing the wages that pay for a premium Christmas turkey. With two years she'd shrink the flock; with five or ten she'd make Megan a partner and share machines with neighbours.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her customers would lose their wages before anyone was ready and the Christmas trade would go with them.
whatWouldHelp: Government backing for small family businesses and apprenticeships, and parishes and neighbours sticking together.
